title: Elementary School Students’ and Teachers’ Perceptions Towards Creative Mathematical Writing with Generative AI
extended_summary:
This paper examines how elementary students and teachers perceived a generative AI-supported creative mathematical writing activity. The authors focus on the pedagogical question of whether GenAI can support young learners in composing math-related stories and how both benefits and challenges are experienced in real classrooms.

The intervention used a researcher-developed GenAI-powered learning platform that guided students through three steps: Ask, Represent, and Transform. Students first unpacked a math story, then represented mathematical ideas visually, and finally co-created culturally relevant math stories with the help of GPT-4 and DALL·E 3. The system also included prompts and a checklist for evaluating AI-generated stories. The study was implemented in six 5th-grade classrooms across two U.S. schools, involving 79 students and six teachers. After several class sessions, 10 students and all six teachers were interviewed; open-ended survey responses and observation notes were used to triangulate the findings.

Using thematic analysis, the authors identified perceived benefits including creativity, mathematical understanding, AI literacy, interest/curiosity, and ownership of learning. They also identified challenges such as weak student critical evaluation of AI output, difficulty generating coherent stories, overly perfect AI responses, limited pedagogical feedback, reduced autonomy, limited social connection, and lack of multiple communication modes. Overall, the paper argues that GenAI can support elementary mathematical writing, but effective educational use depends on careful instructional and interface design that preserves opportunities for human judgment, feedback, and collaboration.

identified_tools.name: GenAI (General)
identified_tools.description: A generative AI-powered learning technology using large language and image generation models to create and revise math stories with supporting prompts and feedback scaffolds.
identified_tools.use_case: Used in elementary classrooms to support 5th-grade students’ creative mathematical writing: students supplied goals, characters, settings, and events; the system generated story drafts and corresponding images; students then evaluated and revised the AI-generated stories.

findings.finding_summary: In a qualitative classroom study with 79 5th-grade students and 6 teachers, participants reported that the GenAI-supported activity fostered creativity in mathematics, including divergent thinking, convergent thinking, originality, and flexible thinking. The paper reports these as thematic findings from interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations; no effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of creativity in mathematical writing

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that the GenAI-supported story-writing process helped students understand math problems, represent mathematical knowledge, and surface misconceptions. Teachers said the Ask and Represent steps supported breakdown of problems and visualization of mathematical ideas; no effect sizes were reported.
findings.measure: Student and teacher perceptions of mathematical understanding and representation

findings.finding_summary: The study found that working with GenAI promoted AI literacy, especially prompt engineering and evaluating AI strengths and weaknesses. This was based on thematic analysis of interview and survey data; no quantitative impact estimate was reported.

Students and teachers perceived improvements in interest, curiosity, and ownership of learning when using the GenAI-supported writing activity. The paper describes these as affective-domain benefits from qualitative data, without effect sizes or statistical tests.
findings.measure: Interest, curiosity, and ownership in learning

findings.finding_summary: The study also identified challenges, including students’ lack of critical evaluation of AI-generated content and difficulty formulating coherent story prompts aligned to learning objectives. These were qualitative barriers reported by students and teachers; no quantitative estimates were provided.
findings.measure: Perceived challenges in critiquing and generating AI-assisted stories

findings.finding_summary: Participants reported that the system lacked pedagogical supports such as adaptive/formative feedback, autonomy-preserving options, social connection features, and multiple communication modes (e.g., speech-to-text). These design limitations were identified through thematic analysis and not measured with numerical outcomes.
findings.measure: Perceived pedagogical/interaction limitations of the system

quality_tier_rationale: This is a qualitative/mixed-method classroom study with interviews, open-ended surveys, and observations rather than a controlled causal design. It provides useful evidence about perceptions and implementation context, but not high-causal-confidence impact estimates.
impact_tier_rationale: The paper reports no effect sizes or statistical impacts, only perceived benefits and challenges. As a result, the practical impact is promising but remains unclear and not quantifiable from the study.
